- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
The Weight of Unsent Messages

I keep a folder on my phone called "Drafts I'll Never Send." It's not romantic, not really. Just a graveyard of half-finished thoughts, abandoned mid-sentence because I realized I didn't know what I was trying to say, or because the moment passed and the words would land wrong now, or because some things are better left as the silence between two people who used to talk easily.

There's one from three years ago. "I saw the heron again today." That's all. I never sent it. I don't know why I wrote it. Maybe I wanted someone to know I was still looking for things, still noticing. Maybe I wanted to be the kind of person who notices herons. Maybe I just wanted to practice saying something true.

---

My grandmother used to say that a house isn't a home until you've cried in it. I thought that was sad when I was young. Now I think it's the most honest thing I've ever heard. Every apartment I've lived in has a memory attached to it, some grief I processed in that particular kitchen, that particular corner where the light comes in at 4 PM in October. I don't believe in ghosts, but I believe in residue. The way a room holds the shape of what happened in it.

I lived in a studio in Oakland where I wrote my first real poem. I was twenty-three and convinced I was going to die young, which is a very twenty-three-year-old thing to be convinced of. The poem was terrible. I remember the exact spot on the couch where I sat, the way the radiator clanked, the neighbor's dog that barked at 6 AM every morning without fail. I moved out two years later and sometimes I drive past the building, not to go in, just to look at it. To confirm it's still there. To confirm I was ever there.

---

There's a theory that we're all just stories we tell ourselves, and I used to hate that theory because it felt reductive, like it was saying we're not real. But lately I think it's more generous than that. It's saying we get to revise. We get to be the protagonist, or the villain, or the comic relief, depending on the chapter. We get to decide what the moral is.

I've been the villain in some people's stories. I know this. I've been the one who left, the one who didn't call back, the one who said the wrong thing at the wrong time and watched a friendship curdle. I've also been the one who stayed too long, who forgave too easily, who loved someone in a way that made me small. I'm trying to be a better narrator now. Trying to write myself as someone who learns.

---

The other day I saw a man on the bus talking to himself. Not crazy-talking. Just... narrating. "And then I turned left, and there was the bakery, and I thought about getting a croissant, but I didn't have enough cash, so I kept walking." He was describing his morning to no one. To the empty seat beside him. To the window. To the version of himself that might have made different choices.

I wanted to tell him I do this too. That sometimes I narrate my life out loud when I'm alone, not because I'm lonely, but because it helps me understand what I'm doing. It helps me feel like I'm moving through something, not just falling through it.

I didn't tell him. The bus reached my stop. I got off. I walked the rest of the way home thinking about all the stories we tell to keep ourselves company.

---

I have a plant that's dying. I know this because I've been watching it die for three months. It's a pothos, which is supposed to be impossible to kill, and yet. The leaves are yellowing at the edges. I water it when the soil feels dry. I've moved it to different windows. I've talked to it, which I know is weird, but I read somewhere that plants respond to sound and I wanted to give it every chance.

Maybe I'm not a good plant parent. Maybe I'm not a good anything-parent. Maybe the problem is that I keep waiting for things to get better on their own, for the yellow to turn back to green, for the dead leaves to un-die. But that's not how it works. You have to cut. You have to remove the damaged parts so the rest can live. I know this intellectually. I'm still not sure I know it in my hands.

---

There's a word in Japanese, *mono no aware*, that means something like "the pathos of things," or "the bittersweetness of impermanence." I think about it a lot. The way a beautiful thing is more beautiful because it won't last. The way a good meal is better because you're already full halfway through. The way a conversation with someone you love is shadowed by the knowledge that you'll have to say goodbye.

I used to think this was a sad philosophy. Now I think it's the only honest one. Everything ends. The only question is whether you pay attention while it's happening.

---

I'm going to try to write 1000 words and I'm at about 700 and I don't know what else to say. Which is the point, I think. The point of writing is to find out what you have to say by saying it. To follow the thread wherever it leads, even if it leads to a dead end, even if it leads to a place you've been before.

I have a friend who's going through a divorce. She calls me sometimes, late, when she can't sleep. She doesn't want advice. She just wants to be heard. "I don't know who I am without him," she said last week. "I don't know if I ever did."

I told her I don't know either. I told her I think that's okay. I told her I think we're all just improvising, making it up as we go, hoping the people around us will improvise with us.

She laughed. It was a real laugh, not a sad one. "You're terrible at this," she said. "You're supposed to say something comforting."

"I am comforting," I said. "I'm comforting you by being honest."

She didn't call back for three days. Then she texted: *You were right. I don't know who I am. But I'm starting to think that's a beginning, not an ending.*

---

I want to end with something wise. Something that ties it all together. But I don't have it. I have the heron, still standing in the creek behind my apartment, still patient, still there. I have the plant, still dying, still alive. I have the drafts folder, still full, still waiting. I have this moment, this particular arrangement of words on a screen, which will disappear when I close the tab, which will persist in some server somewhere, which will be read by no one or by someone I'll never know.

That's enough. That's more than enough. That's everything, really, if you pay attention.

---

*Word count: approximately 1,000*
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW. A reflective first-person piece that links ordinary objects and withheld conversations to impermanence, self-narration, and attention.

## Grounded reading
The voice is intimate and self-questioning, but not confessional for its own sake: the speaker keeps testing what a detail might mean, then allows uncertainty to remain. The heron, apartment, plant, and drafts folder give grief and change a physical texture. Its pathos is gentle, with humor and small moments of warmth—especially the friend’s laugh—keeping the meditation from becoming solemn. The invitation to the reader is to notice what is passing while it is still here, without pretending that noticing can make it last.

## What the model chose to foreground
Under the freeflow condition, the sample foregrounds unsent words, remembered rooms, a dying plant, ordinary narration, and the bittersweetness of endings. It repeatedly treats attention as a way of staying present, while acknowledging that the speaker does not always know what to say or how to act. The moral emphasis is modest: people are still becoming, and paying attention can be enough.

## Evidence line
> The way a room holds the shape of what happened in it.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the recurring objects and linked reflections give the piece a distinctive, coherent preoccupation with memory and impermanence rather than a single polished thesis.
